(1) Major developability risks and structure-based optimization recommendations

The primary risks are low aqueous solubility and insufficient metabolic stability.

Compound A has a thermodynamic solubility of only 20.6 µM at pH 7.4 (approximately 7.4 µg/mL), indicating low solubility that may adversely affect in vivo absorption. Its solubility limitation is primarily lattice-energy-driven (a "brick dust" profile). Consequently, conventional strategies based solely on lowering LogP are likely to provide limited benefit. Optimization should focus on reducing crystal lattice energy and disrupting molecular planarity.

One approach is to introduce an ortho substituent adjacent to the biaryl bond connecting the phenyl ring to C5 of the azaindole core. This would increase the dihedral angle between the rings and disrupt coplanarity. Alternatively, the phenyl ring could be replaced with a saturated or partially saturated linker to increase Fsp³. Polar or ionizable groups could also be introduced in the distal piperazine region, for example by replacing the N-methyl group with N-hydroxyethyl, N-(2-methoxyethyl), or N-(oxetan-3-yl).

The RLM and MLM half-lives are 2.5 min and 4.3 min, respectively, well below commonly accepted levels. The HLM half-life of 23 min is also below the commonly used > 30 min threshold. These results indicate insufficient metabolic stability, making it difficult to meet the TPP requirements for QD oral dosing and long-term treatment of a chronic disease.

Metabolite identification should first establish the actual metabolic soft spots, allowing subsequent structural modifications to target the relevant pathways. Reasonable modifications should then be proposed to block potential metabolic sites at the piperazine alpha-carbons and the N-methyl group, thereby improving metabolic stability.

(2) Interpretation of the efflux ratio discrepancy and choice of absorption prediction model

The difference between MDCK-MDR1 and Caco-2 mainly reflects differences in transporter expression and background passive permeability. MDCK-MDR1 artificially overexpresses human MDR1 at levels far above physiological expression. In addition, MDCK cells have relatively tight junctions and low background passive permeability. Together, these factors systematically elevate the measured efflux ratio. By comparison, transporter expression in Caco-2 is endogenous and closer to physiological conditions. The two results therefore do not constitute a direct contradiction.

Oral absorption prediction should primarily rely on the Caco-2 results. Its Papp A→B of 15 × 10⁻⁶ cm/s indicates high permeability, while an ER of 2.2 indicates limited efflux. Considered together, these results suggest good passive absorption, with P-gp unlikely to be the rate-limiting factor for oral absorption.

The MDCK-MDR1 ER of 27 should be retained as qualitative evidence that compound A has P-gp substrate characteristics. It is relevant to potential tissue distribution liabilities at barriers such as the blood-brain barrier and placenta, rather than to quantitative prediction of intestinal absorption.
